title: Week 1 · Lesson 3: Innate Immunity, Complement & Acute Infection — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 1 — Lesson 3: Innate Immunity, Complement & Acute Infection

FNP-level goal: Understand how the body recognizes infection and tissue damage, connect innate immune signaling to local and systemic findings, and identify when suspected infection requires emergency escalation.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish innate from adaptive immunity.
  • Explain PAMPs, DAMPs, pattern-recognition receptors, cytokines, and complement.
  • Use C3b, C5a, and C5b-9 to reason through opsonization, recruitment, and lysis.
  • Recognize how local infection can progress to sepsis and organ dysfunction.
  • Identify high-risk hosts, appropriate diagnostics, and emergency red flags.

Part 1 — The First Response to Threat

Innate immunity is rapid and pattern-based. Its components include barriers (skin and mucosa), phagocytes, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, complement, cytokines, and vascular/endothelial responses.

Adaptive immunity is antigen-specific and provides memory through B cells, T cells, and antibodies. These systems cooperate; they are not separate clinical silos.

Threat or injury → recognition → innate activation → cytokines/complement → vascular change + leukocyte recruitment → pathogen/debris clearance → resolution and repair.

Part 2 — PAMPs, DAMPs, and Pattern Recognition

PAMPs are conserved pathogen-associated patterns, such as bacterial cell-wall components or viral nucleic acids. DAMPs are endogenous danger signals released or exposed by injured host cells.

Pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs), including Toll-like receptors, allow innate cells to recognize these signals.

PAMP = “possible pathogen.” DAMP = “host tissue injury.” PRR activation = inflammatory program begins.

Clinical implication: inflammation is not synonymous with infection. MI, trauma, pancreatitis, burns, ischemia, autoimmune disease, and malignancy can all generate DAMP-driven inflammation.

Part 3 — Cytokines and the Systemic Response

TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are major inflammatory mediators. They activate endothelium, support leukocyte recruitment, and drive systemic features such as fever and acute-phase responses.

TNF + IL-1 → endothelial activation → leukocyte adhesion and vascular inflammatory response.

IL-6 → liver → acute-phase protein production, including CRP.

CRP is an inflammatory marker, not a diagnosis. It cannot independently distinguish bacterial infection from sterile inflammation or determine whether a patient is stable.

Part 4 — Complement: Three High-Yield Functions

Complement amplifies innate defense through multiple pathways that converge on C3 activation.

  • C3b: opsonization. It coats a pathogen, improving recognition and ingestion by phagocytes. Think: “tag it for eating.”
  • C5a: recruitment and inflammation. It is a powerful chemoattractant and inflammatory signal. Think: “come here.”
  • C5b-9: membrane attack complex (MAC). It forms a pore in susceptible target membranes. Think: “make a hole.”

Complement is protective, but unregulated activation can contribute to inflammation and tissue injury. The lesson is mechanism, not memorization of every pathway protein.

Part 5 — Clinical Connection: Complement Risk

Persistent complement-component deficiency, functional/anatomic asplenia, and complement-inhibiting medications can raise risk for invasive meningococcal disease. A patient receiving a complement inhibitor who has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, rash, confusion, or rapidly progressive illness needs immediate evaluation—not reassurance based on prior vaccination alone.

FNP practice requires medication reconciliation that recognizes immune consequences, vaccination review guided by current recommendations, patient education, and a low threshold for urgent escalation when symptoms suggest invasive infection.

Part 6 — From Bloodstream to Tissue: Neutrophil Recruitment

Acute inflammation commonly features neutrophil recruitment. A useful sequence is:

Margination → rolling → adhesion → diapedesis → chemotaxis.

Cytokine-activated endothelium makes leukocyte adhesion possible. C5a and chemokines guide cells toward the injury. Neutrophils phagocytose and kill microbes using antimicrobial pathways, enzymes, and reactive oxygen species; those same tools can damage surrounding host tissue if activation is excessive.

Part 7 — Why Local Inflammation Looks the Way It Does

Vasodilation → blood flow ↑ → redness and warmth.

Vascular permeability ↑ → protein-rich fluid enters interstitium → edema.

Mediators and increased tissue pressure contribute to pain and loss of function.

These signs confirm an inflammatory response. They do not tell you whether the cause is cellulitis, abscess, DVT, crystal disease, autoimmune disease, ischemia, trauma, or another process.

Part 8 — Fever and Acute-Phase Findings

Inflammatory cytokines promote PGE2-mediated elevation of the hypothalamic temperature set point:

Inflammatory signaling → PGE2 → set point ↑ → fever.

Fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia, and elevated CRP are clues that must be combined with history, examination, site of infection, host risk, vital signs, mental status, and perfusion. Neither a normal white count nor one reassuring measurement excludes serious illness in every patient.

Part 9 — Local Infection to Sepsis

Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. A local infection can progress to systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal vascular tone/permeability, impaired perfusion, and organ dysfunction.

Suspected infection → dysregulated host response → vasodilation/permeability + microcirculatory dysfunction → hypotension and tissue hypoperfusion → organ dysfunction.

FNP assessment includes complete vital signs, mental status, appearance, oxygenation, urine output/history, skin/perfusion, targeted examination, and prompt escalation based on instability. Do not use a single lab, score, or “looks okay” impression to overrule concerning physiology.

Part 10 — Diagnostics: Ask a Clinical Question

Testing depends on suspected source and severity. Possible evaluation includes CBC, metabolic panel, lactate or other perfusion assessment in an acute-care pathway, cultures when indicated, urinalysis/culture, respiratory testing, imaging, ECG, and source-specific studies.

The purpose is to answer: Is infection likely? Where is the source? Is there organ dysfunction or an alternative time-sensitive diagnosis? Does this patient need emergency or hospital-level care?

Part 11 — FNP Disposition

Potential routine outpatient care requires a stable patient, a plausible low-risk diagnosis, no concerning red flags, a clear plan, and reliable follow-up.

Emergency evaluation is appropriate for suspected infection with hypotension, altered mental status, new hypoxemia/respiratory distress, cyanosis or poor perfusion, persistent severe tachycardia, markedly reduced urine output, rapidly progressive rash/soft-tissue symptoms, or concern for meningitis, invasive meningococcal disease, or sepsis.

Part 12 — Board-Style Case 1

A 72-year-old with fever, productive cough, RR 30/min, BP 84/52, confusion, and cool extremities presents after two days of worsening illness.

Mechanism: suspected infection with dysregulated innate response → vascular dysfunction and impaired perfusion → possible sepsis with organ dysfunction.

FNP decision: emergency escalation. This is not a routine pneumonia follow-up or a situation to delay while searching for a single confirmatory test.

Part 13 — Board-Style Case 2

A patient on a C5 complement inhibitor reports abrupt fever, severe headache, vomiting, and a new petechial rash.

Complement blockade raises invasive meningococcal risk. The FNP priority is immediate emergency evaluation and clear handoff about the medication and symptoms.

FNP High-Yield Framework

PAMP/DAMP → PRR → innate activation.

TNF/IL-1 → endothelial activation; IL-6 → acute-phase response.

C3b → opsonization; C5a → chemotaxis/inflammation; C5b-9 → MAC.

Local inflammatory signs are clues, not the final diagnosis.

FNP decision: identify source and host risk, assess perfusion/organ function, consider dangerous alternatives, and escalate immediately for instability or suspected sepsis.
